bull_bear.body: Funding for the greenfield was addressed directly and confidently: cash already received, an **equity raise planned "sometime next year"** sized to need, with **both large shareholders — Vardhman Group and Aichi — having committed to put in as much capital as required**, plus institutional appetite and available bank debt. The Punjab government is described as "very keen" on the project with support "fully assured." The forging project's >10% cost saving (from a INR475cr base) came from renegotiated terms and substituting Indian equipment for Japanese. No dividend or buyback discussion.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation

bull_bear.body:
- **Licence ceiling is the binding constraint.** Growth is capped at ~7–8% until the 3.6-lakh-tonne EC arrives. Management repeated the honest caveat twice: "you haven't got it until you have got it… fingers crossed."
- **Greenfield cost inflation.** Iran-war-driven metal prices and rupee depreciation push cost per tonne up; the scope increase pushes total cost up further. The FY30 commissioning date has not moved yet — watch whether it does.
- **Long dated payback.** The forging plant commissions Q4 FY28 but contributes revenue only from FY30; the greenfield commissions FY30 with revenue FY31. Nothing in the current capex programme materially changes earnings before FY29.
- **Export assumptions already proved wrong.** Management admitted the direct-export thesis was an error — "we had erred. We made a mistake in our assumptions" — and exports will cap near 10%. Customers want Indian *components*, not Indian steel, which is the actual rationale for the forging plant.
- **Advanced Metals is directional only.** No partner, no timeline beyond "a couple of years," and management explicitly told analysts not to model it.
- **Equity dilution ahead** in FY28 for the greenfield.
- **Q1 price settlements incomplete** — some OEMs have not accepted the increase; the Q1 number may be revised upward with the spill-over landing in Q2, which flatters Q2 optically.
bull_bear.title: Risks & watch-items

bull_bear.body: Among the most credible in this batch. Sachit Jain volunteered a downward adjustment to his own EBITDA figure to strip out non-operating treasury income, publicly admitted the export forecast was a mistake, corrected an analyst who mis-stated the greenfield as 5 *million* tonnes with self-deprecating humour ("we have no plans to be big, big boys"), repeatedly caveated the EC approval as not-yet-in-hand, and told investors that the Advanced Metals numbers are too small to bother modelling — the opposite of the usual incentive. He publicly credited the operating team for productivity gains that exceeded what management had thought possible. Guidance is given as ranges with named drivers and revised only with reasoning attached. The one soft spot: no disclosure of net debt, cash, or the funding quantum for the greenfield.
bull_bear.title: Management quality / tone

bull_bear.body:
- The 7–8% growth optics are an artefact of the licence, not of demand. The company is turning orders away and examining outsourced rolling of imported billets to serve customers it cannot supply. Any read of VSSL as a low-growth business misreads a regulatory cap as a demand cap.
- The die-steel move is a realisation story, not a volume story: INR2.5–4 lakh/tonne against a current INR85,000/tonne average, achieved *within* the same 3-lakh-tonne licence. Mix shift is the only growth lever available until the EC lands — which is precisely why ingot casting is being rushed into Q3 FY27.
- The real reason for the forging plant is hidden in the export answer: customers want to buy *components* from India, not steel. The forging unit converts a failed direct-export thesis into an indirect-export franchise. Management has committed to start estimating indirect exports from next quarter — a new disclosure to watch for.
- Seeding non-automotive products now is explicitly about *filling the greenfield faster* later. The FY28 die-steel volumes matter less than the qualifications they generate.
- Green steel is quietly becoming the strongest moat: OEM 2030 targets plus a sole-qualified-supplier position converts an ESG line item into pricing and allocation power, already visible in the Toyota Kirloskar Sambhaji Nagar pull.
- Aichi's surplus funds sitting in Indian money markets are generating enough income that management had to strip it out of EBITDA — an unusual quality-of-earnings tell, disclosed voluntarily.

bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Demand cyclicality and automotive dependence — End-user sectors, particularly automotive, move through cycles and global trade uncertainty increases exposure. The Company's business is closely tied to the four-wheeler industry, so a slowdown in that industry affects performance. Mitigation is a decade-long build of non-automotive presence, a large customer base with confirmed orders and a growing international presence.
- Customer concentration and attrition — Reliance on a few large customers in the automotive value chain could affect stability. Mitigated by a wide customer base of leading OEMs and Tier 1 and 2 players for whom switching time and cost run high, with no single customer accounting for more than 15% of output.
- Capacity and utilisation mismatch — A mismatch among melting, rolling and downstream capacities could constrain growth as demand rises. Melting capacity is described as adequate for the medium term, and the rolling mill expansion to 270,000 TPA aligns steel output with rolled product capacity, capturing profitability that previously went to outsourcing partners. Management separately flags the NDT line and bright bar capacity as the remaining constraints into H1 FY27.
- Quality and product specification risk — Special and alloy steels demand consistently high standards in a specification-driven market. Mitigated by a quality culture reinforced through Aichi-guided SOPs, regular deviation analysis, upgraded testing laboratories, marquee global approvals and IATF 16949 certification.
- Raw material price and foreign exchange volatility — Ferrous scrap, ferro alloys and currency movements in USD, EUR and JPY can affect margins. Mitigated by advance procurement, forward-contract hedging and diversified sourcing including domestic closed-loop initiatives, supported by a zero net debt-to-equity balance sheet.
- Liquidity and funding risk through the expansion cycle — Ongoing expansions and working capital require steady access to capital in a higher-interest-rate environment. Mitigated by financial discipline, internal accruals, a deleveraged balance sheet, regular cash-flow forecasting and access to low-cost banking facilities.
- Environmental and sustainability regulation — Regulation and stakeholder expectations around carbon footprint and resource use continue to rise. Mitigation includes investment in renewable power targeting 40 to 45% of requirements, plus water and energy measures. The bundle truncates mid-sentence at this point, so the full mitigation list was not available.
- Trade barriers, tariffs and export headwinds — U.S. tariffs, a weaker Japanese Yen and trade uncertainty pressured Indian products in some export markets during the year. The MD&A outlook additionally flags tightening EU trade barriers including CBAM, energy cost pressures stemming from the Middle East conflict and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and the risk of redirected Chinese overcapacity as items warranting vigilance.
- Taper of government incentives — Government incentives are expected to taper as the GST refund scheme concludes and solar self-generation reduces electricity duty benefits; the Company expects to absorb this through operating efficiencies and product mix. Read in the MD&A financial review outlook.
bull_bear.title: Bear — key risks

business.body:
- **Automotive alloy steel** — the sole current growth engine, running at licensed capacity. Maruti is ~10% of business today and is the deliberate concentration target going forward; management stressed there is no current customer-concentration risk. The Aichi tie-up delivered global Toyota approval and is delivering the Maruti localisation of imported steels.
- **Non-automotive specialty steel (engine two)** — the FY27–28 build. Route is **ingot casting**, being installed by Q3 FY27. Target products: **die steels** (India imports ~INR1,000cr worth annually), **railway axles**, **windmill shafts** — all import-substitution plays. Economics are transformative on realisation: current average price ~INR85,000/t versus **INR2.5 lakh/t for non-ESR die steel and INR3.5–4 lakh/t as ESR**, though management cautioned costs are also much higher (heat treatment, pressing) so margin does not scale proportionally. Critically, Aichi makes die steels in-house for its own forging (~50% share of the Japanese forging market, 150–170kt), so the know-how is tried and tested.
- **Forging (engine three)** — Technical Assistance Agreement with Aichi Steel signed this quarter; project on schedule and under budget. Ramp will be "very gradual" because it is a new business, but shortened because Vardhman already sends steel to Aichi, gets it forged in Japan and sends the forged product to customers for approval — so process approvals will pre-exist commissioning.
- **Advanced Metals (engine four)** — aerospace and nuclear-plant steels, ~1.5 years away from starting. Explicitly a **non-Aichi JV** (Aichi is strong in automotive, stainless/medical and die steels but not here). Partner search will "take a couple of years"; a separate company because "nobody is going to pass their know-how without being an equal partner." Management pre-emptively told analysts these numbers are "too small and a little outside your horizon."
- **Green steel** — carbon footprint below 0.5 with the necessary approvals, which management claims makes VSSL the **only Indian company able to supply approved green steel**. Toyota Kirloskar's new Sambhaji Nagar (Aurangabad) plant is cited as a specific pull, and most OEMs have 2030 green-steel targets.

With OEM 2030 targets, this is a widening rather than static advantage.

latest_quarter.body: The EBITDA/tonne band is the company's core disclosure discipline, and it is being ratcheted up on four identified levers. Already delivered: the new reheating furnace has improved yields, and the Kocks Block plus reheating furnace took the rolling mill to its 3-lakh-tonne input capacity. Still to come: NDT and peeling lines in-house from Sept/Oct 2026, which eliminates outside job work from Q3 FY27; the solar expansion in ~1–1.5 years; and volume-driven fixed-cost dilution. The pricing mechanism protects the band rather than expanding it — OEMs reset prices on cost parameters, so raw-material inflation flows through rather than compressing margin, with a lag. One caveat management gave on the greenfield: metal prices are up globally and the rupee has depreciated because of the Iran war, so **cost per tonne on the new plant may come in "maybe a little higher"** than envisaged even as scale rises.

outlook.body:
- Move from an automotive steel supplier to a broad special steel provider — management's 'supermarket of special steels' framing — resting on three pillars of capacity, forward integration and diversification.
- Forward integration into forgings with Aichi Steel, starting with a specialised ring gear line using rolling mill technology for passenger car OEMs and Tier 1 suppliers, capturing value previously lost to downstream players.
- Diversify away from automotive dependence by building a non-automotive special steels division for railways, oil and gas, bearings, tool and die steels, with aerospace, defence and nuclear applications planned later; a JV or technical partner is already being sought for these.
- Debottleneck and expand the Ludhiana mother plant while shifting its mix towards more value-added products with complex production routes, since the new greenfield plant will take on the cost-competitive automotive volume.
- Compete on skill rather than price — deliberately leaving the crowded commodity end of the market to others and choosing the narrower, specification-driven path.
- Use green steel credentials as commercial advantage: integrated pricing formulas anchored in green standing with key customers, and CBAM-driven access to European supply chains.
- Deepen localisation with Aichi Steel's support, winning fresh approvals and replacing Japanese-origin steel with domestic steel for domestic OEMs.
- Lift export share using Aichi's global network and the Toyota Production System to win higher-value approvals, widening the bright bar and alloy range to international OEM standards, and promoting green steel and circular economy credentials in regulated markets.
- Scale the closed-loop circular economy model with Maruti Suzuki and extend similar arrangements to additional OEMs.
- Fund the investment cycle conservatively through internal accruals, Vardhman Group support, Aichi Steel participation and, if required, a capital market issue, holding leverage inside the stated ceiling.
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: FY26 completed a debottlenecking cycle at the Ludhiana facility. The Kocks Block three-roll sizing mill was commissioned in the first quarter, holding roundness to +/- 0.2 mm and letting the Company replace imported Japanese steel with domestic steel for domestic OEMs. A walking-beam reheating furnace of 45 TPH from Fives was commissioned in March 2026, lifting rolling capacity from 200,000 tonnes to 270,000 tonnes with full benefits from the second quarter of FY27, extending billet length from 4.2 to 5.2 metres and bringing outside rolling job work in-house. A 40 MW AC solar power plant, set up in partnership with Sone Solar Private Limited with a total investment of Rs 12.45 crores in equity and compulsorily convertible debentures, was commissioned in February 2026 and will meet about 40% of power requirements. Heat size was raised from 37 to 40 tonnes and a 210x210 mm cast section introduced. The second NDT line is on track for commissioning by the second quarter of FY27, with a new peeling line to follow and bright bar shop modernisation planned; management describes the FY27 smaller-project spend as measured, near Rs 100 crore, weighted towards quality and maintenance. Looking further out, three projects define the cycle. A greenfield steel plant set for commissioning in FY30 will produce 500,000 tonnes of billet a year, likely more, in sizes extending beyond the present mill, anchoring a capital cycle worth close to Rs 2,000 crore, funded evenly between equity and debt with leverage held inside a 0.75 ceiling; Aichi Steel has already invested Rs 385 crores as equity, lifting its stake to close to 25%, and management expects commissioning and stabilisation by the end of FY30 with full operational capability from 2030-31. A forging and machining unit built with Aichi Steel at a capex of Rs 475 crore will forge ring gears for the passenger car segment, commissioning by the end of FY2028, led by a senior executive from Aichi. A brownfield melting expansion will raise capacity from 300,000 tonnes to 360,000 tonnes subject to approval from the competent authority, and the Company has decided to apply for environmental clearance for 360,000 tonnes. Ingot casting is planned to start within FY27, with bright bar, heat treatment and cold drawing expanded and a quench and tempering line added, laying the foundation for a non-automotive special steels division. Funding will draw on internal accruals, support from the Vardhman Group, participation from Aichi Steel and, if required, a capital market issue.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- The Company tracks turnover in tonnes shipped rather than rupees, since steel prices move with raw material cycles; revenue followed volume rather than price in FY26 as steel prices eased with softer raw material costs.
- Full-year benefit of the walking-beam reheating furnace, savings from the solar power plant and the shift of job work rolling in-house are expected to lift EBITDA per tonne, with the guidance band moving to Rs 8,000-Rs 11,000 per tonne.
- One factor will temper the gain: government incentives are expected to taper as the GST refund scheme concludes and solar self-generation reduces electricity duty benefits; the Company expects to absorb this through operating efficiencies and product mix.
- The World Steel Association projects India's steel demand to grow 7.4% in 2026 and 9.2% in 2027, the fastest among major economies, with steel demand projected to grow 8-9% in FY27.
- GST 2.0 restructuring effective 22 September 2025 cut GST on small cars and two-wheelers from 28% to 18%, releasing pent-up demand; domestic vehicle wholesales reached a record in FY26 and demand remains strong at the time of writing.
- Automotive premiumisation, electrification, light weighting and enhanced safety standards raise steel intensity per vehicle and are directionally positive for special and alloy steel demand.
- The PLI scheme for specialty steel reinforces policy commitment to import substitution in high-value downstream products.
- Green policy architecture is a demand driver: the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme starting October 2026, the draft Green Public Procurement policy proposing 25-37% low-carbon steel in public infrastructure, and the EU CBAM framework all favour certified low-carbon producers.
- Tool and die steel alone is a sizeable import-substitution opportunity, with around Rs 1,000 crore worth of imports and Aichi Steel holding the know-how for the category.
- Watch items on the outlook: raw material volatility, energy cost pressures from the Middle East conflict, tightening EU trade barriers including CBAM, and the risk of redirected Chinese overcapacity.
- Export headwinds in FY26 from U.S. tariffs, a weaker Japanese Yen and trade uncertainty, offset by improving quality and securing approvals with Aichi Steel's support.
- A large customer base with confirmed orders is cited as holding performance steady through any demand contraction.
- Customers in segments and geographies that did not exist on the order book a year ago are cited in the corporate overview.

deepdive.thesis: The best quarter in the company's history on unit economics — EBITDA/tonne of INR10,760 (INR10,700 excluding non-operating Aichi surplus-fund income) sits at the top of the guided INR8,000–11,000 band, and PAT of INR41cr doubled YoY. The constraint is now regulatory, not commercial: demand is so strong the company is "refusing orders" and running the rolling mill at its 3-lakh-tonne licensed ceiling while the team believes 330,000 tonnes is physically achievable. Management raised the FY28 EBITDA/t band to INR8,000–12,000 and flagged INR9,000–12,000 the year after, and disclosed that the INR475cr forging project will cost **more than 10% less** than budgeted.

risks.note: End-user sectors, particularly automotive, move through cycles and global trade uncertainty increases exposure. The Company's business is closely tied to the four-wheeler industry, so a slowdown in that industry affects performance. Mitigation is a decade-long build of non-automotive presence, a large customer base with confirmed orders and a growing international presence.

Reliance on a few large customers in the automotive value chain could affect stability. Mitigated by a wide customer base of leading OEMs and Tier 1 and 2 players for whom switching time and cost run high, with no single customer accounting for more than 15% of output.

A mismatch among melting, rolling and downstream capacities could constrain growth as demand rises. Melting capacity is described as adequate for the medium term, and the rolling mill expansion to 270,000 TPA aligns steel output with rolled product capacity, capturing profitability that previously went to outsourcing partners. Management separately flags the NDT line and bright bar capacity as the remaining constraints into H1 FY27.

Special and alloy steels demand consistently high standards in a specification-driven market. Mitigated by a quality culture reinforced through Aichi-guided SOPs, regular deviation analysis, upgraded testing laboratories, marquee global approvals and IATF 16949 certification.

Ferrous scrap, ferro alloys and currency movements in USD, EUR and JPY can affect margins. Mitigated by advance procurement, forward-contract hedging and diversified sourcing including domestic closed-loop initiatives, supported by a zero net debt-to-equity balance sheet.

currentContext.strategies: Move from an automotive steel supplier to a broad special steel provider — management's 'supermarket of special steels' framing — resting on three pillars of capacity, forward integration and diversification.|Forward integration into forgings with Aichi Steel, starting with a specialised ring gear line using rolling mill technology for passenger car OEMs and Tier 1 suppliers, capturing value previously lost to downstream players.|Diversify away from automotive dependence by building a non-automotive special steels division for railways, oil and gas, bearings, tool and die steels, with aerospace, defence and nuclear applications planned later; a JV or technical partner is already being sought for these.|Debottleneck and expand the Ludhiana mother plant while shifting its mix towards more value-added products with complex production routes, since the new greenfield plant will take on the cost-competitive automotive volume.|Compete on skill rather than price — deliberately leaving the crowded commodity end of the market to others and choosing the narrower, specification-driven path.|Use green steel credentials as commercial advantage: integrated pricing formulas anchored in green standing with key customers, and CBAM-driven access to European supply chains.|Deepen localisation with Aichi Steel's support, winning fresh approvals and replacing Japanese-origin steel with domestic steel for domestic OEMs.|Lift export share using Aichi's global network and the Toyota Production System to win higher-value approvals, widening the bright bar and alloy range to international OEM standards, and promoting green steel and circular economy credentials in regulated markets.|Scale the closed-loop circular economy model with Maruti Suzuki and extend similar arrangements to additional OEMs.|Fund the investment cycle conservatively through internal accruals, Vardhman Group support, Aichi Steel participation and, if required, a capital market issue, holding leverage inside the stated ceiling.
currentContext.expansion: FY26 completed a debottlenecking cycle at the Ludhiana facility. The Kocks Block three-roll sizing mill was commissioned in the first quarter, holding roundness to +/- 0.2 mm and letting the Company replace imported Japanese steel with domestic steel for domestic OEMs. A walking-beam reheating furnace of 45 TPH from Fives was commissioned in March 2026, lifting rolling capacity from 200,000 tonnes to 270,000 tonnes with full benefits from the second quarter of FY27, extending billet length from 4.2 to 5.2 metres and bringing outside rolling job work in-house. A 40 MW AC solar power plant, set up in partnership with Sone Solar Private Limited with a total investment of Rs 12.45 crores in equity and compulsorily convertible debentures, was commissioned in February 2026 and will meet about 40% of power requirements. Heat size was raised from 37 to 40 tonnes and a 210x210 mm cast section introduced. The second NDT line is on track for commissioning by the second quarter of FY27, with a new peeling line to follow and bright bar shop modernisation planned; management describes the FY27 smaller-project spend as measured, near Rs 100 crore, weighted towards quality and maintenance. Looking further out, three projects define the cycle. A greenfield steel plant set for commissioning in FY30 will produce 500,000 tonnes of billet a year, likely more, in sizes extending beyond the present mill, anchoring a capital cycle worth close to Rs 2,000 crore, funded evenly between equity and debt with leverage held inside a 0.75 ceiling; Aichi Steel has already invested Rs 385 crores as equity, lifting its stake to close to 25%, and management expects commissioning and stabilisation by the end of FY30 with full operational capability from 2030-31. A forging and machining unit built with Aichi Steel at a capex of Rs 475 crore will forge ring gears for the passenger car segment, commissioning by the end of FY2028, led by a senior executive from Aichi. A brownfield melting expansion will raise capacity from 300,000 tonnes to 360,000 tonnes subject to approval from the competent authority, and the Company has decided to apply for environmental clearance for 360,000 tonnes. Ingot casting is planned to start within FY27, with bright bar, heat treatment and cold drawing expanded and a quench and tempering line added, laying the foundation for a non-automotive special steels division. Funding will draw on internal accruals, support from the Vardhman Group, participation from Aichi Steel and, if required, a capital market issue.
currentContext.mdna: The Company tracks turnover in tonnes shipped rather than rupees, since steel prices move with raw material cycles; revenue followed volume rather than price in FY26 as steel prices eased with softer raw material costs.|Full-year benefit of the walking-beam reheating furnace, savings from the solar power plant and the shift of job work rolling in-house are expected to lift EBITDA per tonne, with the guidance band moving to Rs 8,000-Rs 11,000 per tonne.|One factor will temper the gain: government incentives are expected to taper as the GST refund scheme concludes and solar self-generation reduces electricity duty benefits; the Company expects to absorb this through operating efficiencies and product mix.|The World Steel Association projects India's steel demand to grow 7.4% in 2026 and 9.2% in 2027, the fastest among major economies, with steel demand projected to grow 8-9% in FY27.|GST 2.0 restructuring effective 22 September 2025 cut GST on small cars and two-wheelers from 28% to 18%, releasing pent-up demand; domestic vehicle wholesales reached a record in FY26 and demand remains strong at the time of writing.|Automotive premiumisation, electrification, light weighting and enhanced safety standards raise steel intensity per vehicle and are directionally positive for special and alloy steel demand.|The PLI scheme for specialty steel reinforces policy commitment to import substitution in high-value downstream products.|Green policy architecture is a demand driver: the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme starting October 2026, the draft Green Public Procurement policy proposing 25-37% low-carbon steel in public infrastructure, and the EU CBAM framework all favour certified low-carbon producers.|Tool and die steel alone is a sizeable import-substitution opportunity, with around Rs 1,000 crore worth of imports and Aichi Steel holding the know-how for the category.|Watch items on the outlook: raw material volatility, energy cost pressures from the Middle East conflict, tightening EU trade barriers including CBAM, and the risk of redirected Chinese overcapacity.|Export headwinds in FY26 from U.S. tariffs, a weaker Japanese Yen and trade uncertainty, offset by improving quality and securing approvals with Aichi Steel's support.|A large customer base with confirmed orders is cited as holding performance steady through any demand contraction.|Customers in segments and geographies that did not exist on the order book a year ago are cited in the corporate overview.

risks.note: End-user sectors, particularly automotive, move through cycles and global trade uncertainty increases exposure. The Company's business is closely tied to the four-wheeler industry, so a slowdown in that industry affects performance. Mitigation is a decade-long build of non-automotive presence, a large customer base with confirmed orders and a growing international presence.

Reliance on a few large customers in the automotive value chain could affect stability. Mitigated by a wide customer base of leading OEMs and Tier 1 and 2 players for whom switching time and cost run high, with no single customer accounting for more than 15% of output.

A mismatch among melting, rolling and downstream capacities could constrain growth as demand rises. Melting capacity is described as adequate for the medium term, and the rolling mill expansion to 270,000 TPA aligns steel output with rolled product capacity, capturing profitability that previously went to outsourcing partners. Management separately flags the NDT line and bright bar capacity as the remaining constraints into H1 FY27.

Special and alloy steels demand consistently high standards in a specification-driven market. Mitigated by a quality culture reinforced through Aichi-guided SOPs, regular deviation analysis, upgraded testing laboratories, marquee global approvals and IATF 16949 certification.

risks.risk: Raw material price and foreign exchange volatility
risks.note: Ferrous scrap, ferro alloys and currency movements in USD, EUR and JPY can affect margins. Mitigated by advance procurement, forward-contract hedging and diversified sourcing including domestic closed-loop initiatives, supported by a zero net debt-to-equity balance sheet.

risks.risk: Liquidity and funding risk through the expansion cycle
risks.note: Ongoing expansions and working capital require steady access to capital in a higher-interest-rate environment. Mitigated by financial discipline, internal accruals, a deleveraged balance sheet, regular cash-flow forecasting and access to low-cost banking facilities.

Regulation and stakeholder expectations around carbon footprint and resource use continue to rise. Mitigation includes investment in renewable power targeting 40 to 45% of requirements, plus water and energy measures. The bundle truncates mid-sentence at this point, so the full mitigation list was not available.

risks.risk: Trade barriers, tariffs and export headwinds
risks.note: U.S. tariffs, a weaker Japanese Yen and trade uncertainty pressured Indian products in some export markets during the year. The MD&A outlook additionally flags tightening EU trade barriers including CBAM, energy cost pressures stemming from the Middle East conflict and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and the risk of redirected Chinese overcapacity as items warranting vigilance.

Government incentives are expected to taper as the GST refund scheme concludes and solar self-generation reduces electricity duty benefits; the Company expects to absorb this through operating efficiencies and product mix. Read in the MD&A financial review outlook.

one-line thesis: The best quarter in the company's history on unit economics — EBITDA/tonne of INR10,760 (INR10,700 excluding non-operating Aichi surplus-fund income) sits at the top of the guided INR8,000–11,000 band, and PAT of INR41cr doubled YoY. The constraint is now regulatory, not commercial: demand is so strong the company is "refusing orders" and running the rolling mill at its 3-lakh-tonne licensed ceiling while the team believes 330,000 tonnes is physically achievable. Management raised the FY28 EBITDA/t band to INR8,000–12,000 and flagged INR9,000–12,000 the year after, and disclosed that the INR475cr forging project will cost **more than 10% less** than budgeted.

guidance (critical — verify next quarter:
- **Volume:** **~255,000 t for FY27**; **>270,000 t in FY28**, rising to **~290,000 t in FY28 if the environmental clearance lands** (production can improve to that level without further capex); **330,000–340,000 t by FY29** once new capex is installed.
- **Margin (the headline commitment):** EBITDA/t range moves from the current **INR8,000–11,000 to INR8,000–12,000 in FY28**, and management intends to raise the floor to **INR9,000–12,000 in FY29** once the new solar plant commissions. Four named drivers: (i) fixed-cost dilution on higher volume, (ii) operating costs already falling, (iii) job work / outside processing coming in-house **from Q3 FY27**, (iv) new solar capacity ~a year out.
- **Pricing:** **Q2 FY27 realisations will be higher than Q1** — a price increase has been sought effective 1 July. Q1 settlements are incomplete with some OEMs and are "likely to rise higher," with the spill-over landing in Q2. Q3 expected flat to marginally either way, depending on raw material.
- **Capex / commissioning dates:**
  - **New NDT line and new peeling line — commissioned by September/October 2026.** These remove the current bottleneck (finished material piling up awaiting testing capacity, and peeling being job-worked outside).
  - **Ingot casting — established by Q3 FY27, stabilised by Q4 FY27**; enables **regular die-steel production in FY28**.
  - **Environmental clearance for melting capacity 3.0 → 3.6 lakh t — approval expected "in the next 3, 4 months."**
  - **Forging unit (with Aichi) — commissioning in Q4 FY28**; 6–12 months to fill the plant; **revenue from end-FY29 / FY30**. **Project cost more than 10% below the INR475cr estimate.**
  - **Greenfield steel plant (Punjab, 5 lakh t, being upsized) — land and machinery to be finalised by end-August, latest mid-September 2026**; **commissioning FY30 (financial year '29-'30)**; 6–8 months to stabilise; **revenues from FY31**.
  - **Solar plant capacity +~50% in about 1 to 1.5 years** (savings per unit lower than phase 1 because of new domestic-cell content rules).
  - **European OEM commercial supply — expected in H2 FY27** ("later part of this financial year"); samples already sent.
  - **Maruti import-substitution commercial production — starts Q4 FY27.**
- **Capital raising:** an equity raise **"sometime next year"** (FY28), timing dependent on funding need. Vardhman Group and Aichi have both committed to subscribe as required; institutional appetite exists; debt described as available.
- **Exports:** deliberately capped — "At max, it will go up to about 10%."
order book & pipeline: There is no order book by design: "we never have a strong output — there is no system of a very strong order book… no customer gives long-term orders." The relevant statement is the inverse — the company is **completely booked out and refusing orders**, and is "finding it difficult to meet the requirements of the customers." Management is even examining importing billets and rolling them on job work outside to service demand it cannot make in-house, contingent on finding a credible supply chain. The next identified volume step-up is Maruti import substitution beginning commercial production in Q4 FY27.
segment / subsidiary detail:
- **Automotive alloy steel** — the sole current growth engine, running at licensed capacity. Maruti is ~10% of business today and is the deliberate concentration target going forward; management stressed there is no current customer-concentration risk. The Aichi tie-up delivered global Toyota approval and is delivering the Maruti localisation of imported steels.
- **Non-automotive specialty steel (engine two)** — the FY27–28 build. Route is **ingot casting**, being installed by Q3 FY27. Target products: **die steels** (India imports ~INR1,000cr worth annually), **railway axles**, **windmill shafts** — all import-substitution plays. Economics are transformative on realisation: current average price ~INR85,000/t versus **INR2.5 lakh/t for non-ESR die steel and INR3.5–4 lakh/t as ESR**, though management cautioned costs are also much higher (heat treatment, pressing) so margin does not scale proportionally. Critically, Aichi makes die steels in-house for its own forging (~50% share of the Japanese forging market, 150–170kt), so the know-how is tried and tested.
- **Forging (engine three)** — Technical Assistance Agreement with Aichi Steel signed this quarter; project on schedule and under budget. Ramp will be "very gradual" because it is a new business, but shortened because Vardhman already sends steel to Aichi, gets it forged in Japan and sends the forged product to customers for approval — so process approvals will pre-exist commissioning.
- **Advanced Metals (engine four)** — aerospace and nuclear-plant steels, ~1.5 years away from starting. Explicitly a **non-Aichi JV** (Aichi is strong in automotive, stainless/medical and die steels but not here). Partner search will "take a couple of years"; a separate company because "nobody is going to pass their know-how without being an equal partner." Management pre-emptively told analysts these numbers are "too small and a little outside your horizon."
- **Green steel** — carbon footprint below 0.5 with the necessary approvals, which management claims makes VSSL the **only Indian company able to supply approved green steel**. Toyota Kirloskar's new Sambhaji Nagar (Aurangabad) plant is cited as a specific pull, and most OEMs have 2030 green-steel targets.
growth verticals / optionality: The four-engine framing is the cleanest strategic articulation on the call: (1) automotive steel today, (2) non-automotive specialty steel from FY28, (3) forging from FY29–30, (4) advanced metals ~1.5 years out and beyond. The non-obvious purpose of engine two was stated plainly — volumes will be low initially, but **seeding these products now means the new 5-lakh-tonne plant can be filled faster** once it commissions, because the business will already be established and qualified.
6a. moat & competitive position:
- **Green-steel monopoly, claimed and specific.** "Our carbon footprint is below 0.5… there isn't any other company which is near us in carbon footprint, which has the approvals." Two commercial consequences were evidenced: a strong position for European exports, and being the only qualified supplier for Toyota Kirloskar's expansion. With OEM 2030 targets, this is a widening rather than static advantage.
- **Aichi Steel as a technology and approval channel.** Global Toyota approval and the Maruti localisation mandate were both attributed directly to the partnership. For die steels specifically, foreign know-how is described as essential, and Aichi has it in production use.
- **Renewable cost position.** 43% of power from solar with a further ~50% capacity expansion planned — a structural cost advantage in an energy-intensive process.
- **Pricing pass-through structure.** OEM contracts move price up or down with raw-material cost, which is *why* the company can guide an EBITDA/tonne band at all: "We remain protected within a range."
margins & cost dynamics: The EBITDA/tonne band is the company's core disclosure discipline, and it is being ratcheted up on four identified levers. Already delivered: the new reheating furnace has improved yields, and the Kocks Block plus reheating furnace took the rolling mill to its 3-lakh-tonne input capacity. Still to come: NDT and peeling lines in-house from Sept/Oct 2026, which eliminates outside job work from Q3 FY27; the solar expansion in ~1–1.5 years; and volume-driven fixed-cost dilution. The pricing mechanism protects the band rather than expanding it — OEMs reset prices on cost parameters, so raw-material inflation flows through rather than compressing margin, with a lag. One caveat management gave on the greenfield: metal prices are up globally and the rupee has depreciated because of the Iran war, so **cost per tonne on the new plant may come in "maybe a little higher"** than envisaged even as scale rises.

Slippage watch: the greenfield is being *re-scoped upward* (more testing lines, higher capacity, scrap preheating) with a revised project presented at the next board meeting — cost and capacity both rising, commissioning still held at FY30.
capital allocation: Funding for the greenfield was addressed directly and confidently: cash already received, an **equity raise planned "sometime next year"** sized to need, with **both large shareholders — Vardhman Group and Aichi — having committed to put in as much capital as required**, plus institutional appetite and available bank debt. The Punjab government is described as "very keen" on the project with support "fully assured." The forging project's >10% cost saving (from a INR475cr base) came from renegotiated terms and substituting Indian equipment for Japanese. No dividend or buyback discussion.
risks & watch-items:
- **Licence ceiling is the binding constraint.** Growth is capped at ~7–8% until the 3.6-lakh-tonne EC arrives. Management repeated the honest caveat twice: "you haven't got it until you have got it… fingers crossed."
- **Greenfield cost inflation.** Iran-war-driven metal prices and rupee depreciation push cost per tonne up; the scope increase pushes total cost up further. The FY30 commissioning date has not moved yet — watch whether it does.
- **Long dated payback.** The forging plant commissions Q4 FY28 but contributes revenue only from FY30; the greenfield commissions FY30 with revenue FY31. Nothing in the current capex programme materially changes earnings before FY29.
- **Export assumptions already proved wrong.** Management admitted the direct-export thesis was an error — "we had erred. We made a mistake in our assumptions" — and exports will cap near 10%. Customers want Indian *components*, not Indian steel, which is the actual rationale for the forging plant.
- **Advanced Metals is directional only.** No partner, no timeline beyond "a couple of years," and management explicitly told analysts not to model it.
- **Equity dilution ahead** in FY28 for the greenfield.
- **Q1 price settlements incomplete** — some OEMs have not accepted the increase; the Q1 number may be revised upward with the spill-over landing in Q2, which flatters Q2 optically.
management quality / tone: Among the most credible in this batch. Sachit Jain volunteered a downward adjustment to his own EBITDA figure to strip out non-operating treasury income, publicly admitted the export forecast was a mistake, corrected an analyst who mis-stated the greenfield as 5 *million* tonnes with self-deprecating humour ("we have no plans to be big, big boys"), repeatedly caveated the EC approval as not-yet-in-hand, and told investors that the Advanced Metals numbers are too small to bother modelling — the opposite of the usual incentive. He publicly credited the operating team for productivity gains that exceeded what management had thought possible. Guidance is given as ranges with named drivers and revised only with reasoning attached. The one soft spot: no disclosure of net debt, cash, or the funding quantum for the greenfield.
non-obvious takeaways:
- The 7–8% growth optics are an artefact of the licence, not of demand. The company is turning orders away and examining outsourced rolling of imported billets to serve customers it cannot supply. Any read of VSSL as a low-growth business misreads a regulatory cap as a demand cap.
- The die-steel move is a realisation story, not a volume story: INR2.5–4 lakh/tonne against a current INR85,000/tonne average, achieved *within* the same 3-lakh-tonne licence. Mix shift is the only growth lever available until the EC lands — which is precisely why ingot casting is being rushed into Q3 FY27.
- The real reason for the forging plant is hidden in the export answer: customers want to buy *components* from India, not steel. The forging unit converts a failed direct-export thesis into an indirect-export franchise. Management has committed to start estimating indirect exports from next quarter — a new disclosure to watch for.
- Seeding non-automotive products now is explicitly about *filling the greenfield faster* later. The FY28 die-steel volumes matter less than the qualifications they generate.
- Green steel is quietly becoming the strongest moat: OEM 2030 targets plus a sole-qualified-supplier position converts an ESG line item into pricing and allocation power, already visible in the Toyota Kirloskar Sambhaji Nagar pull.
- Aichi's surplus funds sitting in Indian money markets are generating enough income that management had to strip it out of EBITDA — an unusual quality-of-earnings tell, disclosed voluntarily.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: Vardhman Special Steels Limited is a Vardhman Group company making premium special and alloy steels at Ludhiana for India's automotive value chain, with a technical and equity alliance with Aichi Steel Corporation of the Toyota Group.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: The Company manufactures premium special steels via the Electric Arc Furnace route using scrap as its primary feedstock at a single integrated plant in Ludhiana, Punjab, alongside its corporate headquarters. Output is billets, hot-rolled bars and bright bars sold to automotive OEMs, Tier 1 and Tier 2 component makers in India and to export markets, chiefly ASEAN. A technical alliance with Aichi Steel Corporation, a Toyota Group member that has since taken an equity stake, brings Toyota-standard metallurgical practice and is the base for a move downstream into forgings.

segment_detail.title: Segment / subsidiary detail
segment_detail.body:
- **Automotive alloy steel** — the sole current growth engine, running at licensed capacity. Maruti is ~10% of business today and is the deliberate concentration target going forward; management stressed there is no current customer-concentration risk. The Aichi tie-up delivered global Toyota approval and is delivering the Maruti localisation of imported steels.
- **Non-automotive specialty steel (engine two)** — the FY27–28 build. Route is **ingot casting**, being installed by Q3 FY27. Target products: **die steels** (India imports ~INR1,000cr worth annually), **railway axles**, **windmill shafts** — all import-substitution plays. Economics are transformative on realisation: current average price ~INR85,000/t versus **INR2.5 lakh/t for non-ESR die steel and INR3.5–4 lakh/t as ESR**, though management cautioned costs are also much higher (heat treatment, pressing) so margin does not scale proportionally. Critically, Aichi makes die steels in-house for its own forging (~50% share of the Japanese forging market, 150–170kt), so the know-how is tried and tested.
- **Forging (engine three)** — Technical Assistance Agreement with Aichi Steel signed this quarter; project on schedule and under budget. Ramp will be "very gradual" because it is a new business, but shortened because Vardhman already sends steel to Aichi, gets it forged in Japan and sends the forged product to customers for approval — so process approvals will pre-exist commissioning.
- **Advanced Metals (engine four)** — aerospace and nuclear-plant steels, ~1.5 years away from starting. Explicitly a **non-Aichi JV** (Aichi is strong in automotive, stainless/medical and die steels but not here). Partner search will "take a couple of years"; a separate company because "nobody is going to pass their know-how without being an equal partner." Management pre-emptively told analysts these numbers are "too small and a little outside your horizon."
- **Green steel** — carbon footprint below 0.5 with the necessary approvals, which management claims makes VSSL the **only Indian company able to supply approved green steel**. Toyota Kirloskar's new Sambhaji Nagar (Aurangabad) plant is cited as a specific pull, and most OEMs have 2030 green-steel targets.

guidance.title: Guidance (CRITICAL — verify next quarter)
guidance.body:
- **Volume:** **~255,000 t for FY27**; **>270,000 t in FY28**, rising to **~290,000 t in FY28 if the environmental clearance lands** (production can improve to that level without further capex); **330,000–340,000 t by FY29** once new capex is installed.
- **Margin (the headline commitment):** EBITDA/t range moves from the current **INR8,000–11,000 to INR8,000–12,000 in FY28**, and management intends to raise the floor to **INR9,000–12,000 in FY29** once the new solar plant commissions. Four named drivers: (i) fixed-cost dilution on higher volume, (ii) operating costs already falling, (iii) job work / outside processing coming in-house **from Q3 FY27**, (iv) new solar capacity ~a year out.
- **Pricing:** **Q2 FY27 realisations will be higher than Q1** — a price increase has been sought effective 1 July. Q1 settlements are incomplete with some OEMs and are "likely to rise higher," with the spill-over landing in Q2. Q3 expected flat to marginally either way, depending on raw material.
- **Capex / commissioning dates:**
  - **New NDT line and new peeling line — commissioned by September/October 2026.** These remove the current bottleneck (finished material piling up awaiting testing capacity, and peeling being job-worked outside).
  - **Ingot casting — established by Q3 FY27, stabilised by Q4 FY27**; enables **regular die-steel production in FY28**.
  - **Environmental clearance for melting capacity 3.0 → 3.6 lakh t — approval expected "in the next 3, 4 months."**
  - **Forging unit (with Aichi) — commissioning in Q4 FY28**; 6–12 months to fill the plant; **revenue from end-FY29 / FY30**. **Project cost more than 10% below the INR475cr estimate.**
  - **Greenfield steel plant (Punjab, 5 lakh t, being upsized) — land and machinery to be finalised by end-August, latest mid-September 2026**; **commissioning FY30 (financial year '29-'30)**; 6–8 months to stabilise; **revenues from FY31**.
  - **Solar plant capacity +~50% in about 1 to 1.5 years** (savings per unit lower than phase 1 because of new domestic-cell content rules).
  - **European OEM commercial supply — expected in H2 FY27** ("later part of this financial year"); samples already sent.
  - **Maruti import-substitution commercial production — starts Q4 FY27.**
- **Capital raising:** an equity raise **"sometime next year"** (FY28), timing dependent on funding need. Vardhman Group and Aichi have both committed to subscribe as required; institutional appetite exists; debt described as available.

The non-obvious purpose of engine two was stated plainly — volumes will be low initially, but **seeding these products now means the new 5-lakh-tonne plant can be filled faster** once it commissions, because the business will already be established and qualified.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- The Company tracks turnover in tonnes shipped rather than rupees, since steel prices move with raw material cycles; revenue followed volume rather than price in FY26 as steel prices eased with softer raw material costs.
- Full-year benefit of the walking-beam reheating furnace, savings from the solar power plant and the shift of job work rolling in-house are expected to lift EBITDA per tonne, with the guidance band moving to Rs 8,000-Rs 11,000 per tonne.
- One factor will temper the gain: government incentives are expected to taper as the GST refund scheme concludes and solar self-generation reduces electricity duty benefits; the Company expects to absorb this through operating efficiencies and product mix.
- The World Steel Association projects India's steel demand to grow 7.4% in 2026 and 9.2% in 2027, the fastest among major economies, with steel demand projected to grow 8-9% in FY27.
- GST 2.0 restructuring effective 22 September 2025 cut GST on small cars and two-wheelers from 28% to 18%, releasing pent-up demand; domestic vehicle wholesales reached a record in FY26 and demand remains strong at the time of writing.
- Automotive premiumisation, electrification, light weighting and enhanced safety standards raise steel intensity per vehicle and are directionally positive for special and alloy steel demand.
- The PLI scheme for specialty steel reinforces policy commitment to import substitution in high-value downstream products.
- Green policy architecture is a demand driver: the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme starting October 2026, the draft Green Public Procurement policy proposing 25-37% low-carbon steel in public infrastructure, and the EU CBAM framework all favour certified low-carbon producers.
- Tool and die steel alone is a sizeable import-substitution opportunity, with around Rs 1,000 crore worth of imports and Aichi Steel holding the know-how for the category.
- Watch items on the outlook: raw material volatility, energy cost pressures from the Middle East conflict, tightening EU trade barriers including CBAM, and the risk of redirected Chinese overcapacity.
- Export headwinds in FY26 from U.S. tariffs, a weaker Japanese Yen and trade uncertainty, offset by improving quality and securing approvals with Aichi Steel's support.
- A large customer base with confirmed orders is cited as holding performance steady through any demand contraction.
- Customers in segments and geographies that did not exist on the order book a year ago are cited in the corporate overview.

margins.title: Margins & cost dynamics
margins.body: The EBITDA/tonne band is the company's core disclosure discipline, and it is being ratcheted up on four identified levers. Already delivered: the new reheating furnace has improved yields, and the Kocks Block plus reheating furnace took the rolling mill to its 3-lakh-tonne input capacity. Still to come: NDT and peeling lines in-house from Sept/Oct 2026, which eliminates outside job work from Q3 FY27; the solar expansion in ~1–1.5 years; and volume-driven fixed-cost dilution. The pricing mechanism protects the band rather than expanding it — OEMs reset prices on cost parameters, so raw-material inflation flows through rather than compressing margin, with a lag. One caveat management gave on the greenfield: metal prices are up globally and the rupee has depreciated because of the Iran war, so **cost per tonne on the new plant may come in "maybe a little higher"** than envisaged even as scale rises.

capital_allocation.title: Capital allocation
capital_allocation.body: Funding for the greenfield was addressed directly and confidently: cash already received, an **equity raise planned "sometime next year"** sized to need, with **both large shareholders — Vardhman Group and Aichi — having committed to put in as much capital as required**, plus institutional appetite and available bank debt. The Punjab government is described as "very keen" on the project with support "fully assured." The forging project's >10% cost saving (from a INR475cr base) came from renegotiated terms and substituting Indian equipment for Japanese. No dividend or buyback discussion.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: FY26 completed a debottlenecking cycle at the Ludhiana facility. The Kocks Block three-roll sizing mill was commissioned in the first quarter, holding roundness to +/- 0.2 mm and letting the Company replace imported Japanese steel with domestic steel for domestic OEMs. A walking-beam reheating furnace of 45 TPH from Fives was commissioned in March 2026, lifting rolling capacity from 200,000 tonnes to 270,000 tonnes with full benefits from the second quarter of FY27, extending billet length from 4.2 to 5.2 metres and bringing outside rolling job work in-house. A 40 MW AC solar power plant, set up in partnership with Sone Solar Private Limited with a total investment of Rs 12.45 crores in equity and compulsorily convertible debentures, was commissioned in February 2026 and will meet about 40% of power requirements. Heat size was raised from 37 to 40 tonnes and a 210x210 mm cast section introduced. The second NDT line is on track for commissioning by the second quarter of FY27, with a new peeling line to follow and bright bar shop modernisation planned; management describes the FY27 smaller-project spend as measured, near Rs 100 crore, weighted towards quality and maintenance. Looking further out, three projects define the cycle. A greenfield steel plant set for commissioning in FY30 will produce 500,000 tonnes of billet a year, likely more, in sizes extending beyond the present mill, anchoring a capital cycle worth close to Rs 2,000 crore, funded evenly between equity and debt with leverage held inside a 0.75 ceiling; Aichi Steel has already invested Rs 385 crores as equity, lifting its stake to close to 25%, and management expects commissioning and stabilisation by the end of FY30 with full operational capability from 2030-31. A forging and machining unit built with Aichi Steel at a capex of Rs 475 crore will forge ring gears for the passenger car segment, commissioning by the end of FY2028, led by a senior executive from Aichi. A brownfield melting expansion will raise capacity from 300,000 tonnes to 360,000 tonnes subject to approval from the competent authority, and the Company has decided to apply for environmental clearance for 360,000 tonnes. Ingot casting is planned to start within FY27, with bright bar, heat treatment and cold drawing expanded and a quench and tempering line added, laying the foundation for a non-automotive special steels division. Funding will draw on internal accruals, support from the Vardhman Group, participation from Aichi Steel and, if required, a capital market issue.

management_tone.title: Management quality / tone
management_tone.body: Among the most credible in this batch. Sachit Jain volunteered a downward adjustment to his own EBITDA figure to strip out non-operating treasury income, publicly admitted the export forecast was a mistake, corrected an analyst who mis-stated the greenfield as 5 *million* tonnes with self-deprecating humour ("we have no plans to be big, big boys"), repeatedly caveated the EC approval as not-yet-in-hand, and told investors that the Advanced Metals numbers are too small to bother modelling — the opposite of the usual incentive. He publicly credited the operating team for productivity gains that exceeded what management had thought possible. Guidance is given as ranges with named drivers and revised only with reasoning attached. The one soft spot: no disclosure of net debt, cash, or the funding quantum for the greenfield.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Technical and equity alliance with Aichi Steel Corporation of the Toyota Group, which raised its stake to 24.90% in July 2025 and brings Toyota Production System discipline, forging know-how and access to global customer approvals
- Carbon intensity of 0.73 tCO2/tonne in FY26 falling to 0.45-0.48 post-solar, against a government green steel norm of 2.2 and major domestic competitors at 3.0 and above — a green steel credential management describes as a passport into European supply chains under CBAM
- High switching costs: consistent product quality has built a wide customer base of leading OEMs and Tier 1 and 2 players for whom the time and cost of switching vendors run high
- Customer diversification within automotive — no single customer accounts for more than 15% of output
- Closed-loop circular economy arrangement with Maruti Suzuki, live since September 2025, securing a high-quality scrap stream and anchoring the Company as both buyer and supplier in the customer's chain
- In-house R&D delivering import-substitute grades, with total R&D spend at 1.03% of turnover in FY26 versus 0.83% in FY25
- Kocks Block three-roll rolling technology holding roundness to +/- 0.2 mm, enabling replacement of imported Japanese steel with domestic steel for domestic OEMs
- Debt-free balance sheet during FY26 with a net debt-to-equity ratio of 0.00x, and a stated intent to hold leverage inside a 0.75 ceiling through the investment cycle

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body:
- **Licence ceiling is the binding constraint.** Growth is capped at ~7–8% until the 3.6-lakh-tonne EC arrives. Management repeated the honest caveat twice: "you haven't got it until you have got it… fingers crossed."
- **Greenfield cost inflation.** Iran-war-driven metal prices and rupee depreciation push cost per tonne up; the scope increase pushes total cost up further. The FY30 commissioning date has not moved yet — watch whether it does.
- **Long dated payback.** The forging plant commissions Q4 FY28 but contributes revenue only from FY30; the greenfield commissions FY30 with revenue FY31. Nothing in the current capex programme materially changes earnings before FY29.
- **Export assumptions already proved wrong.** Management admitted the direct-export thesis was an error — "we had erred. We made a mistake in our assumptions" — and exports will cap near 10%. Customers want Indian *components*, not Indian steel, which is the actual rationale for the forging plant.
- **Advanced Metals is directional only.** No partner, no timeline beyond "a couple of years," and management explicitly told analysts not to model it.
- **Equity dilution ahead** in FY28 for the greenfield.
- **Q1 price settlements incomplete** — some OEMs have not accepted the increase; the Q1 number may be revised upward with the spill-over landing in Q2, which flatters Q2 optically.

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body:
- The 7–8% growth optics are an artefact of the licence, not of demand. The company is turning orders away and examining outsourced rolling of imported billets to serve customers it cannot supply. Any read of VSSL as a low-growth business misreads a regulatory cap as a demand cap.
- The die-steel move is a realisation story, not a volume story: INR2.5–4 lakh/tonne against a current INR85,000/tonne average, achieved *within* the same 3-lakh-tonne licence. Mix shift is the only growth lever available until the EC lands — which is precisely why ingot casting is being rushed into Q3 FY27.
- The real reason for the forging plant is hidden in the export answer: customers want to buy *components* from India, not steel. The forging unit converts a failed direct-export thesis into an indirect-export franchise. Management has committed to start estimating indirect exports from next quarter — a new disclosure to watch for.
- Seeding non-automotive products now is explicitly about *filling the greenfield faster* later. The FY28 die-steel volumes matter less than the qualifications they generate.
- Green steel is quietly becoming the strongest moat: OEM 2030 targets plus a sole-qualified-supplier position converts an ESG line item into pricing and allocation power, already visible in the Toyota Kirloskar Sambhaji Nagar pull.
- Aichi's surplus funds sitting in Indian money markets are generating enough income that management had to strip it out of EBITDA — an unusual quality-of-earnings tell, disclosed voluntarily.

Critically, Aichi makes die steels in-house for its own forging (~50% share of the Japanese forging market, 150–170kt), so the know-how is tried and tested.
- **Forging (engine three)** — Technical Assistance Agreement with Aichi Steel signed this quarter; project on schedule and under budget. Ramp will be "very gradual" because it is a new business, but shortened because Vardhman already sends steel to Aichi, gets it forged in Japan and sends the forged product to customers for approval — so process approvals will pre-exist commissioning.
- **Advanced Metals (engine four)** — aerospace and nuclear-plant steels, ~1.5 years away from starting. Explicitly a **non-Aichi JV** (Aichi is strong in automotive, stainless/medical and die steels but not here). Partner search will "take a couple of years"; a separate company because "nobody is going to pass their know-how without being an equal partner." Management pre-emptively told analysts these numbers are "too small and a little outside your horizon."
- **Green steel** — carbon footprint below 0.5 with the necessary approvals, which management claims makes VSSL the **only Indian company able to supply approved green steel**. Toyota Kirloskar's new Sambhaji Nagar (Aurangabad) plant is cited as a specific pull, and most OEMs have 2030 green-steel targets.
growth verticals / optionality: The four-engine framing is the cleanest strategic articulation on the call: (1) automotive steel today, (2) non-automotive specialty steel from FY28, (3) forging from FY29–30, (4) advanced metals ~1.5 years out and beyond. The non-obvious purpose of engine two was stated plainly — volumes will be low initially, but **seeding these products now means the new 5-lakh-tonne plant can be filled faster** once it commissions, because the business will already be established and qualified.
6a. moat & competitive position:
- **Green-steel monopoly, claimed and specific.** "Our carbon footprint is below 0.5… there isn't any other company which is near us in carbon footprint, which has the approvals." Two commercial consequences were evidenced: a strong position for European exports, and being the only qualified supplier for Toyota Kirloskar's expansion. With OEM 2030 targets, this is a widening rather than static advantage.
- **Aichi Steel as a technology and approval channel.** Global Toyota approval and the Maruti localisation mandate were both attributed directly to the partnership. For die steels specifically, foreign know-how is described as essential, and Aichi has it in production use.
- **Renewable cost position.** 43% of power from solar with a further ~50% capacity expansion planned — a structural cost advantage in an energy-intensive process.
- **Pricing pass-through structure.** OEM contracts move price up or down with raw-material cost, which is *why* the company can guide an EBITDA/tonne band at all: "We remain protected within a range."
margins & cost dynamics: The EBITDA/tonne band is the company's core disclosure discipline, and it is being ratcheted up on four identified levers. Already delivered: the new reheating furnace has improved yields, and the Kocks Block plus reheating furnace took the rolling mill to its 3-lakh-tonne input capacity. Still to come: NDT and peeling lines in-house from Sept/Oct 2026, which eliminates outside job work from Q3 FY27; the solar expansion in ~1–1.5 years; and volume-driven fixed-cost dilution. The pricing mechanism protects the band rather than expanding it — OEMs reset prices on cost parameters, so raw-material inflation flows through rather than compressing margin, with a lag. One caveat management gave on the greenfield: metal prices are up globally and the rupee has depreciated because of the Iran war, so **cost per tonne on the new plant may come in "maybe a little higher"** than envisaged even as scale rises.

Slippage watch: the greenfield is being *re-scoped upward* (more testing lines, higher capacity, scrap preheating) with a revised project presented at the next board meeting — cost and capacity both rising, commissioning still held at FY30.
capital allocation: Funding for the greenfield was addressed directly and confidently: cash already received, an **equity raise planned "sometime next year"** sized to need, with **both large shareholders — Vardhman Group and Aichi — having committed to put in as much capital as required**, plus institutional appetite and available bank debt. The Punjab government is described as "very keen" on the project with support "fully assured." The forging project's >10% cost saving (from a INR475cr base) came from renegotiated terms and substituting Indian equipment for Japanese. No dividend or buyback discussion.
risks & watch-items:
- **Licence ceiling is the binding constraint.** Growth is capped at ~7–8% until the 3.6-lakh-tonne EC arrives. Management repeated the honest caveat twice: "you haven't got it until you have got it… fingers crossed."
- **Greenfield cost inflation.** Iran-war-driven metal prices and rupee depreciation push cost per tonne up; the scope increase pushes total cost up further. The FY30 commissioning date has not moved yet — watch whether it does.
- **Long dated payback.** The forging plant commissions Q4 FY28 but contributes revenue only from FY30; the greenfield commissions FY30 with revenue FY31. Nothing in the current capex programme materially changes earnings before FY29.
- **Export assumptions already proved wrong.** Management admitted the direct-export thesis was an error — "we had erred. We made a mistake in our assumptions" — and exports will cap near 10%. Customers want Indian *components*, not Indian steel, which is the actual rationale for the forging plant.
- **Advanced Metals is directional only.** No partner, no timeline beyond "a couple of years," and management explicitly told analysts not to model it.
- **Equity dilution ahead** in FY28 for the greenfield.
- **Q1 price settlements incomplete** — some OEMs have not accepted the increase; the Q1 number may be revised upward with the spill-over landing in Q2, which flatters Q2 optically.
management quality / tone: Among the most credible in this batch. Sachit Jain volunteered a downward adjustment to his own EBITDA figure to strip out non-operating treasury income, publicly admitted the export forecast was a mistake, corrected an analyst who mis-stated the greenfield as 5 *million* tonnes with self-deprecating humour ("we have no plans to be big, big boys"), repeatedly caveated the EC approval as not-yet-in-hand, and told investors that the Advanced Metals numbers are too small to bother modelling — the opposite of the usual incentive. He publicly credited the operating team for productivity gains that exceeded what management had thought possible. Guidance is given as ranges with named drivers and revised only with reasoning attached. The one soft spot: no disclosure of net debt, cash, or the funding quantum for the greenfield.
non-obvious takeaways:
- The 7–8% growth optics are an artefact of the licence, not of demand. The company is turning orders away and examining outsourced rolling of imported billets to serve customers it cannot supply. Any read of VSSL as a low-growth business misreads a regulatory cap as a demand cap.
- The die-steel move is a realisation story, not a volume story: INR2.5–4 lakh/tonne against a current INR85,000/tonne average, achieved *within* the same 3-lakh-tonne licence. Mix shift is the only growth lever available until the EC lands — which is precisely why ingot casting is being rushed into Q3 FY27.
- The real reason for the forging plant is hidden in the export answer: customers want to buy *components* from India, not steel. The forging unit converts a failed direct-export thesis into an indirect-export franchise. Management has committed to start estimating indirect exports from next quarter — a new disclosure to watch for.
- Seeding non-automotive products now is explicitly about *filling the greenfield faster* later. The FY28 die-steel volumes matter less than the qualifications they generate.
- Green steel is quietly becoming the strongest moat: OEM 2030 targets plus a sole-qualified-supplier position converts an ESG line item into pricing and allocation power, already visible in the Toyota Kirloskar Sambhaji Nagar pull.
- Aichi's surplus funds sitting in Indian money markets are generating enough income that management had to strip it out of EBITDA — an unusual quality-of-earnings tell, disclosed voluntarily.
